story.title: The one-shot begins as a sealed delivery
story.statement: Goldspire Messengers starts as a paid delivery through a dangerous managed forest.
story.body: Player-safe hook: the package matters, the forest is old, and the job will get stranger. Do not introduce the hidden contents or late-act reveal from the standby screen.
story.say: "Tonight starts with a simple job: take a sealed package through a huge old forest and get paid when it arrives."
story.ask: If someone asks what the story is about: "A delivery job, a sealed package, a forest route, and the question of who gets protected when business and magic collide."
story.deeper: Player-safe hook: the package matters, the forest is old, and the job will get stranger. Do not introduce the hidden contents or late-act reveal from the standby screen.

mechanic.title: Standby is table-readiness and player-display orientation
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is room setup: players learn where to look and how the session will be paced.
mechanic.body: This beat trains the table to treat the TV as shared focus while keeping decisions and private prompts on the GM side.
mechanic.say: "For now, just let the screen cycle. Once we begin, I will use it like a live slideshow: sometimes image, sometimes text, sometimes a quick prompt."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks whether they need rules now: "No. I will teach the rules when the first risky moment needs them."
mechanic.deeper: This beat trains the table to treat the TV as shared focus while keeping decisions and private prompts on the GM side.

title: Welcome, Logistics, and GM Role
alt: Session Zero welcome and logistics icon.
caption: Cover room logistics, the GM role, the player role, and the shape of an in-person one-shot before teaching rules.
gmGoal: Cover room logistics, the GM role, the player role, and the shape of an in-person one-shot before teaching rules.
publicObjective: This is a standalone one-shot at Mox. We are here to tell a complete story tonight, learn the game as we go, and make sure everyone has enough information to participate comfortably.
readAloud: This is a standalone one-shot at Mox. We are here to tell a complete story tonight, learn the game as we go, and make sure everyone has enough information to participate comfortably.
playerBullets: Your GM is Kyle, he/him. Kyle has 15+ years running in-person and online TTRPGs.
GM style for Daggerheart: story-first, roleplay-friendly, and mechanics in service of the table's fun.
Kyle plays the world, keeps the rules moving, asks questions, and helps everyone get spotlight.
You play one character. Say what they try to do, ask questions, and make choices from their point of view.
We will confirm session length, end time, breaks, bathrooms, drinks, and any Mox house policies before we begin.
Phones are fine for reference or emergencies. Please keep attention at the table when another player has the spotlight.
This is a complete story tonight: Session Zero, opening job, rising trouble, final pressure, and a short closeout if time allows.

gmNotes: Script: Welcome everyone by name if possible. Say: I'm Kyle, he/him, and you can call me Kyle. I've been running TTRPGs for 15+ years, both in person and online. For Daggerheart, my style is story-first and roleplay-friendly: the mechanics are here to support the table's fun and help us resolve risky moments, not to make you memorize a rulebook. I play the world, frame scenes, make rulings, and help everyone get time in the spotlight. You play one character and tell me what they try to do. Before we begin, let's confirm end time, breaks, bathrooms, drinks, phone expectations, and any Mox house policies.
This card exists before safety and rules so strangers know what room they are in.
Keep it practical. The table needs confidence, not a speech.

Checklist: Introduce yourself as GM; Name/pronouns: Kyle, he/him; Mention 15+ years running in-person and online TTRPGs; State story-first, roleplay-friendly Daggerheart style; Confirm headcount, seats, names, and any latecomers; Confirm session length and target end time; Cover Mox house policies or ask staff if needed; Point out bathrooms, drinks, and table logistics; Set phone policy: reference and emergencies are fine, attention stays at the table; State that tonight is a standalone complete story
GM-only: Ask May or Mox staff for current house policies before the event if they are not already posted.

player.title: Players know who Kyle is
player.statement: Players know Kyle's name, pronouns, experience, and GM style.
player.body: This cue gives Kyle credibility and lowers pressure for beginners: story-forward, mechanics-assisted, and open to interruption.
player.say: "I am Kyle, he/him. I have run tabletop games for more than fifteen years, and tonight my job is to help the table tell a strong story without making rules feel like homework."
player.ask: If someone asks how strict the rules will be: "I care about the rules when they help the scene. If a rule would slow us down, I will make a clear ruling and keep us moving."
player.deeper: This cue gives Kyle credibility and lowers pressure for beginners: story-forward, mechanics-assisted, and open to interruption.

story.title: The night is a complete one-shot
story.statement: This is a full one-shot with a beginning, middle, and end.
story.body: Use this to prevent campaign-pitch drift. The table should feel that their choices matter tonight.
story.say: "Tonight is built to complete a story at the table: onboarding, contract, road trouble, village pressure, reveal, and final choice."
story.ask: If a player asks whether this becomes a campaign: "Tonight stands alone. If people love it, there are future threads, but you will get a complete arc now."
story.deeper: Use this to prevent campaign-pitch drift. The table should feel that their choices matter tonight.

mechanic.title: GM role and player role are established
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is spotlight contract: Kyle frames scenes; players drive characters.
mechanic.body: This is the first spotlight-sharing cue. It tells players they do not need to perform constantly, but they are allowed to enter the scene.
mechanic.say: "I play the world and keep the pace. You play one character and tell me what they do, ask, feel, and risk."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks when they should talk: "When your character reacts, wants something, notices something, or has a question, jump in. I will help balance spotlight."
mechanic.deeper: This is the first spotlight-sharing cue. It tells players they do not need to perform constantly, but they are allowed to enter the scene.

Use the answers to decide how slowly to teach dice, sheet reading, and spotlight combat.

player.title: Players meet each other before characters
player.statement: Players introduce themselves as people before performing a role.
player.body: The useful output is not biography; it is calibration. Kyle learns who needs more rules support, who wants roleplay, and who may need gentler spotlight.
player.say: "Before characters, let us meet the people. Name, pronouns if you want, your tabletop experience level, and one thing you hope we get tonight."
player.ask: If someone hesitates: "You can keep it tiny: name, whether you are new or experienced, and one word for the vibe you like."
player.deeper: The useful output is not biography; it is calibration. Kyle learns who needs more rules support, who wants roleplay, and who may need gentler spotlight.

story.title: The table becomes an ensemble
story.statement: The table becomes a temporary ensemble before the fiction begins.
story.body: This is the social foundation for character connections later; shy players get seen before they are asked to improvise.
story.say: "This is a group story. Before we ask the characters to trust each other, I want the players to know who is sharing the table."
story.ask: If someone asks why this matters: "It helps me pace explanations, invite people in, and make sure the game serves the people actually here."
story.deeper: This is the social foundation for character connections later; shy players get seen before they are asked to improvise.

mechanic.title: Beginner calibration and spotlight pacing
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is table calibration: Kyle learns how much support and spotlight each player wants.
mechanic.body: Treat this as the first pass-and-return demonstration. The table learns that passing is allowed and not a failure.
mechanic.say: "If you are new, I will explain more. If you are experienced, I may ask you to help model play without taking over."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks whether they can pass: "Yes. Say pass, and I will come back to you after a couple of people go."
mechanic.deeper: Treat this as the first pass-and-return demonstration. The table learns that passing is allowed and not a failure.

playerBullets: Concept: a corporate-fantasy delivery job that becomes morally complicated.
Aim: learn Daggerheart, build the party, protect a community, and discover what the sealed delivery means.
Tone: mostly sincere fantasy adventure, with corporate satire and dark whimsy around the edges.

gmScript: Name the Concept, Aim, Tone, and Subject Matter without using the acronym as shorthand. Ask whether anything in the subject matter list needs a line, veil, or softer framing.
gmReadAloud: Here is the frame for tonight. The concept is a corporate-fantasy delivery job that becomes morally complicated. The aim is to learn Daggerheart, build a party that can work together, protect a community, and discover what this sealed delivery really means. The tone is mostly sincere fantasy adventure with corporate satire and a little dark whimsy around the edges. The subject matter can include fantasy danger, ambush, death, corporate exploitation, undead, memory or fear magic, and optional animal peril. If anything in that list needs to be offscreen, softened, or redirected, tell me now or at any point during play.

player.say: "This is a corporate-fantasy delivery job: sincere adventure, strange forest, dangerous choices, and a little satire around the paperwork."
player.ask: If a player asks what their character should care about: "Care about the job, the people beside you, and what feels wrong once the route starts talking back."
player.deeper: The frame is CATS without the acronym: what we are playing, what we want, how it should feel, and what content might appear.

story.title: Goldspire is paperwork plus magic
story.statement: The job crosses a fantasy region where paperwork and magic collide.
story.body: Use plain terms before proper nouns. The players need the feel of the place before names like Sablewood or Emeris matter.
story.say: "The world has old magic, living forests, and companies trying to turn all of that into routes, contracts, and profit."
story.ask: If players ask what Goldspire is: "Think fantasy logistics territory: roads, signs, permits, villages, old places, and companies pretending they own more than they understand."
story.deeper: Use plain terms before proper nouns. The players need the feel of the place before names like Sablewood or Emeris matter.

mechanic.title: CATS is table calibration
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is calibration: the group agrees what kind of play is welcome tonight.
mechanic.body: This is not a lecture. It gives players an immediate way to shape tone and subject matter without derailing the game.
mechanic.say: "If something I name sounds like too much, tell me now or later. We can soften, skip, or move it offscreen."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks whether they have to disclose personal limits: "No details required. You can just say soften that, skip that, or not for me."
mechanic.deeper: This is not a lecture. It gives players an immediate way to shape tone and subject matter without derailing the game.

player.title: Players know how to pause or step away

player.body: This is the in-person safety kit: open door, pause, rewind, soften, break, slow down, repeat, and no dumb questions.

story.title: The real table outranks fictional danger
story.statement: The real table stays safer than any fictional danger.
story.body: Use this line before danger enters so later safety adjustments feel normal instead of exceptional.
story.say: "The story can put characters in danger. The people at this table are not in danger. If the fiction stops being fun or clear, we adjust."
story.ask: If someone asks whether pausing ruins the scene: "No. Pausing protects the scene because it lets us continue with trust."
story.deeper: Use this line before danger enters so later safety adjustments feel normal instead of exceptional.

mechanic.title: Safety tools are table permissions
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is live table communication.
mechanic.body: These permissions also help accessibility and comprehension, not only discomfort.
mechanic.say: "If I move too fast, interrupt me. If you are confused, ask. If something feels bad, say pause. Those are all valid moves."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks what words to use: "Pause means stop now; rewind means back up and redo; soften means keep the idea but lower the intensity; break means step away."
mechanic.deeper: These permissions also help accessibility and comprehension, not only discomfort.

title: Player Expectations / Shared Table Care
playerTitle: How we make this fun together
alt: Shared table participation icon.
caption: Set player expectations for participation, shared care, questions, and communication.
gmGoal: Set player expectations for participation, shared care, questions, and communication.
publicObjective: This works best when everyone is engaged, respectful, and helping the table have fun. You are responsible for your own fun and for noticing the other people at the table too.
readAloud: This works best when everyone is engaged, respectful, and helping the table have fun. You are responsible for your own fun and for noticing the other people at the table too.
playerBullets: Engage with the story and ask questions.
Invite other players in: ask them what their character thinks, notices, or does.
Speak when it is your turn, and be mindful of how much space you are taking.
Only participate at the level you are comfortable with.
Tell me if you are confused, uncomfortable, not having fun, or need help.
I will do my best to engage everyone, but the table works because we all pay attention to each other.
If there is time at the end, we may do quick Stars and Wishes: one thing you liked, one thing you would want more or different next time.

playerTable.meaning: Questions are welcome at any time.

player.title: Players know fun is shared work
player.statement: Players know to ask, listen, invite, make room, and speak up.
player.body: The table expectation is active generosity: not constant talking, not silence, but shared attention.
player.say: "Everyone is here for everyone. Make room, ask each other questions, listen when someone has spotlight, and speak up when you need help."
player.ask: If someone asks what good participation looks like: "Take your turn, invite someone else in, and stay curious about what the other characters do."
player.deeper: The table expectation is active generosity: not constant talking, not silence, but shared attention.

story.title: The party works because players engage
story.statement: The party will work because the players pay attention to each other.
story.body: This protects the one-shot from lone-wolf drift and keeps character conflict collaborative.
story.say: "The party does not have to agree on everything, but the players are building something together. Let other characters matter to yours."
story.ask: If someone asks about intra-party conflict: "Tension is fine. Undermining another player's fun is not. Check in before pushing hard."
story.deeper: This protects the one-shot from lone-wolf drift and keeps character conflict collaborative.

mechanic.title: Spotlight sharing is a table mechanic
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is spotlight: take space, make space, and pass when needed.
mechanic.body: This is also Kyle's self-check: slow down, stop interrupting, and let silence do some work.
mechanic.say: "If you have had a big moment, look for someone to hand the next moment to. If you have been quiet, I may invite you in."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks whether they can pass: "Yes. You can pass, and I will come back to you. Passing is a pacing tool, not a failure."
mechanic.deeper: This is also Kyle's self-check: slow down, stop interrupting, and let silence do some work.

alt: Rules reference icon for Daggerheart basics.
caption: Teach the minimum Daggerheart rules needed to begin.
gmGoal: Teach the minimum Daggerheart rules needed to begin.
publicObjective: Daggerheart is narrative fantasy. The GM describes the world, players describe what their characters do, and we roll when the outcome is risky, uncertain, or dramatic.
readAloud: Daggerheart is narrative fantasy. The GM describes the world, players describe what their characters do, and we roll when the outcome is risky, uncertain, or dramatic.
playerBullets: Describe what your character tries to do.
If it is risky or uncertain, roll Hope and Fear d12s.
Add the trait that fits your approach.
Tell the GM the total and whether Hope or Fear was higher.
We will learn the rest as it matters.
gmNotes: Script: Teach only the minimum rules, then move on. Open the GM Rules Drawer for deeper questions, but do not dump the full rulebook before play.
Every rules term should link to the GM Rules Drawer in GM view.
Do not present non-official or stale mechanics as official Daggerheart rules.
Checklist: Duality Dice explained; Hope/Fear explained; Experiences explained; Helping explained; Outcome matrix explained
Rules snapshot: Duality Dice; Hope; Fear; Action Rolls; Experiences; Helping; Difficulty Ladder; Combat Spotlight

gmScript: Teach only the minimum rules, then move on. Open the GM Rules Drawer for deeper questions, but do not dump the full rulebook before play.
gmReadAloud: Here is the minimum Daggerheart loop. Tell me what your character wants to do. If the outcome is risky, uncertain, or dramatic, I will ask for a roll. Most rolls use two d12s: one Hope die and one Fear die. You add the right trait from your sheet and compare the total to a Difficulty. The total tells us whether you succeed. The higher die tells us whether the result comes with Hope or Fear. Doubles are a Critical Success. You do not need to remember all of that right now; I will walk you through it when the first roll happens.

player.title: Players know the Daggerheart loop
player.statement: Players know describe action, roll when risky, read Hope or Fear.
player.body: Minimum loop: fiction first, dice second, total for success, higher die for Hope/Fear, doubles for Critical Success.
player.say: "Tell me what you do. If it is risky or uncertain, roll two d12s, add the right trait, and tell me the total and which die is higher."
player.ask: If someone asks what Hope and Fear mean: "Hope means the result tilts toward you and you may gain Hope. Fear means the result gives me a GM resource or complication."
player.deeper: Minimum loop: fiction first, dice second, total for success, higher die for Hope/Fear, doubles for Critical Success.

story.title: The system supports cinematic consequences
story.statement: Daggerheart supports choices and consequences rather than tactical homework.
story.body: This lets D&D players map old instincts while learning what is different.
story.say: "The dice do not replace the story. They tell us what your risky choice costs, reveals, or changes."
story.ask: If someone asks if this is like Dungeons & Dragons: "Close enough to feel familiar, but the Hope/Fear dice make the tone of success or failure matter immediately."
story.deeper: This lets D&D players map old instincts while learning what is different.

mechanic.statement: Players get the minimum rules needed for the first roll.

mechanic.say: "For the first roll, I will name the trait and difficulty. You roll Hope and Fear, add the trait, and we read the result together."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks for the difficulty ladder: "Easy is 10, standard is 15, hard is 20. I will tell you the number when it matters."
mechanic.deeper: Mention sheet sections only as needed: traits modify rolls; Experiences can help when relevant; Stress, HP, and Armor matter once danger starts.

gmNotes: Script: Use the prompt bank and Connection Builder. Ask each player for at least one connection in quick mode. Save accepted, clarified, complicated, or passed results.

Show players only the active prompt and permission language, not the whole GM prompt bank.

Checklist: At least one connection target per player; Connection Builder entries saved; Group memory asked if time allows; Ask one optional world-connection question per player if the table has energy.; Log answers as table-contributed canon when they point at a faction, NPC, or location.
gmScript: Use the prompt bank and Connection Builder. Ask each player for at least one connection in quick mode. Save accepted, clarified, complicated, or passed results.
gmReadAloud: Connections are quick relationship prompts. One player offers a memory or relationship question, and another player answers from their character's point of view. You are not writing someone else's character. You are offering a hook. The other player can accept it, clarify it, complicate it, soften it, or pass. We only need enough connection to make the party feel like people who can start the job together.
gmChecklist: At least one connection target per player
Connection Builder entries saved
Group memory asked if time allows
Ask one optional world-connection question per player if the table has energy.
Log answers as table-contributed canon when they point at a faction, NPC, or location.
gmExamples: World connection example: "Somebody you knew got buried in debt. Who were they, and who held the note?" The answer becomes table canon and can attach to Goldwater, Soulspire, or another fitting faction.
World connection example: "What slogan have you heard too many times?" Use the player's answer to make the next faction feel like it has already touched their life.
Rules-backed pattern: one player offers a first-person shared-history prompt, another player answers from their character's memory, and anyone can turn down a bad fit.
Module example: Marlowe can use 'I owe you a favor.' Ask another PC what happened, then let them accept, clarify, complicate, soften, or pass.
P2P example: 'We've run a delivery that went wrong before. What did we agree never to tell anyone?' Keep the answer short enough to play tonight.
playerTakeaway: Players can create connections by offering, accepting, clarifying, complicating, softening, or passing.
storyTakeaway: The PCs enter the job with at least one relationship already alive.

player.statement: Players can offer, accept, clarify, complicate, soften, or pass.
player.body: Per-character prompt banks are available in the per-character layer. Use one prompt per player if time is tight.
player.say: "A connection is an offer, not a command. Ask another player a relationship question; they can accept it, adjust it, complicate it, soften it, or pass."

story.title: The party starts with one live relationship
story.statement: The PCs enter the job with at least one relationship already alive.
story.body: Connection output should be playable tonight: a favor, suspicion, rescue, shared job, protected secret, or misjudgment.
story.say: "You do not have to be best friends. We just need one thread that makes the crew feel like people with history before the job starts."
story.ask: If players worry about overwriting each other: "Make it a memory from your character's point of view. The other player decides what is true for their character."
story.deeper: Connection output should be playable tonight: a favor, suspicion, rescue, shared job, protected secret, or misjudgment.

mechanic.title: Connection prompts are relationship mechanics
mechanic.statement: Connection prompts build party relationships before play begins.
mechanic.body: The mechanic is consent-based relationship creation: offer, answer, adjust, record, play.
mechanic.say: "Ask the prompt, let the other player answer, then write down the useful part in one sentence."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks if the answer gives a bonus: "Tonight it mainly gives us story leverage and spotlight. If a sheet feature calls for a connection later, we will use it then."
mechanic.deeper: The mechanic is consent-based relationship creation: offer, answer, adjust, record, play.

playerQuestions: There is a company everyone in the territories deals with that you personally do not trust. What is it to you, and what did it cost you?
You have carried freight before. Tell me about the one parcel you wish you had never agreed to move.
Somebody you knew got buried in debt they could not climb out of. Who were they to you, and who held the note?
What slogan have you heard so many times you can recite it in your sleep, and how do you feel when you hear it now?
You have met one of the undead laborers up close. What did that encounter leave you believing?
Name a place out here that felt wrong the moment you stepped into it. What was off?
Who taught you not to trust the people in nice livery? What happened to them?
What small kindness did a stranger do for you on the road that you have never forgotten?

title: What PCs Know
alt: A player-safe route gate map for the delivery through Sablewood.
caption: Align starting knowledge without leaking hidden information.
gmGoal: Align starting knowledge without leaking hidden information.
publicObjective: You are on a delivery job to the village of Hush. The cargo is sealed, valuable, and not supposed to be opened without permission.
readAloud: You are on a delivery job to the village of Hush. The cargo is sealed, valuable, and not supposed to be opened without permission.
playerBullets: You are escorting one sealed cargo unit.
It is important, guarded, and not supposed to be opened without permission.
It is going to Hush, a village in the Goldspire Territories.
The route crosses Sablewood Logistics Preserve: a vast fantasy forest, called Old Sable by some locals.
Payment follows verified delivery.
You begin inside the system: loyal, ignorant, conflicted, pragmatic, or simply hired.

mechanicTakeaway: Separates player-safe starting knowledge from GM-only mystery.

player.title: Players know starting facts only
player.statement: Players know the starting facts without hidden GM answers.
player.body: This is where lore overload gets prevented. Players know enough to act and enough not to feel stupid asking basic questions.
player.say: "Starting facts: you have a sealed important package, a paid delivery job, a huge old forest route, and a village destination. The rest is allowed to be unknown."
player.ask: If someone asks whether their character should know the names: "If it makes sense, you may know the company name, the village name, or the forest name, but you are still new to this specific route."
player.deeper: This is where lore overload gets prevented. Players know enough to act and enough not to feel stupid asking basic questions.

story.title: Known route, unknown truth
story.statement: They escort a sealed package to a forest village through a huge old forest.
story.body: Use plain descriptions before proper nouns: company, old forest, village, sealed package. Names can arrive through play.
story.say: "The job is simple at the surface: get the package to the village. The truth underneath it is what play will uncover."
story.ask: If someone asks what is inside the package: "You do not know yet. Marlowe knows it matters; Varian, Khari, and others may notice physical clues once they see it."
story.deeper: Use plain descriptions before proper nouns: company, old forest, village, sealed package. Names can arrive through play.

mechanic.title: Starting knowledge is a play boundary
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is separating known facts from discoverable mystery.
mechanic.body: This teaches question-driven discovery before the Prologue starts.
mechanic.say: "If you wonder whether your character knows something, ask me. I will either answer, give you the player-safe version, or call for a Knowledge or Instinct roll."
mechanic.ask: If someone asks how to learn more: "Ask a contact, inspect an object, compare it to your background, or roll when the answer is uncertain."
mechanic.deeper: This teaches question-driven discovery before the Prologue starts.

Varian can catch a wrong-mineral scent with Instinct 13. Khari can tell it is heavier than ordinary cargo with Strength or Instinct 13."

mechanic.title: Unknowns convert through questions and rolls

mechanic.deeper: Good early difficulties: 10 for obvious sensory foreshadowing, 13 for social or character-specific reads, 14 for spotting the official story as too neat.

player.deeper: Use this cue when players feel under-informed. The intended feeling is professional uncertainty, not confusion: they have a job, a contact, a package, and permission to ask practical questions.

story.title: Ordinary contract first, deeper truth later

story.body: Do not say Keystone Asset here. The Prologue should make the mystery physical: a crate, a contract, a route, and a contact who knows more than the paper says.

story.deeper: Do not say Keystone Asset here. The Prologue should make the mystery physical: a crate, a contract, a route, and a contact who knows more than the paper says.

mechanic.title: Question-driven play starts now

Reveal omitted risk or fine print.
Make the human cost visible before escalating danger.

choicesConsequences.consequence: They get names and practical facts, plus one doubt-flicker.
The run starts clean and professional.
The seal flares and logs the attempt.
choicesConsequences.payoff: Later corporate attention becomes easier to justify.

lootClues: Authorized route copy
Emergency toll voucher
A private worry from the contact, if roleplayed for

Keystone Asset™: Inside the sealed crate, packed in wax-paper and reassurance, sits a heavy grey stone the size of a loaf, warm to the touch, faintly humming, with a light deep inside it that is slowly going out.

storyScope.antagonist_line: Perceived antagonist: the forest. True antagonist: the corporate lie about the forest. The players never confront it directly. They are meant to feel it by the end.
storyScope.gm_thesis: Every act offers at least one guaranteed and one earned hint that the danger is manufactured and the forest is not the enemy.

act_seeds.text: Grail-branded bounty board: "STRIXWOLF: APEX FOREST HAZARD. Sightings up 300%. Bounty payable in Marks."
Couriers or a clerk trade fearful route gossip: the Preserve "takes one a week now."
A player asking what they know receives the corporate line: strixwolves are vicious pack predators.

pacing.label: Onboarding + Prologue
pacing.context: pregens, safety, connections, Contract overview, Job briefing, forest threshold
pacing.lever: Keep the Contract to plain setup, let the Job carry questions, then move to the blocked road.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Arcana, ward-sense, and the custodian responsibility around the package.
perCharacterLayer.passive: She is the custodian. Give her the bonus insight: the package is the priority, Emeris chose her specifically, and the cargo feels warded even while sealed.

discover.text: Marlowe only: this is her extra Arcana check in module language; in Daggerheart terms, use Knowledge. The crate hums with old, high-tier ward-magic meant for a serious public ward. Do not reveal the Treehouse truth yet.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: She can answer some crew questions the contact deflects because she has been read in further than a hired agent.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Marlowe, the sealed crate hums with old ward-magic. You still do not know exactly what is inside, but you know this package is the priority.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Shadows, deals, underworld instinct, and noticing when a job smells wrong.
perCharacterLayer.passive: The crate's seal is official, but the load-in was rushed. Someone packed this in a hurry.

discover.text: He clocks either a hidden compartment in the carriage or that the contact carries more coin than a simple courier run should require.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: He can negotiate the terms with Strike a Deal: better pay, a loosened clause, or a clearer risk answer.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Barnacle, the seal looks official, but the load-in was rushed. Someone wanted this packed and moving fast.

perCharacterLayer.ancestryClass: Highborne Human Warrior, Call of the Brave
perCharacterLayer.lane: Threat-reading, escort habits, social warmth, and de-escalation.
perCharacterLayer.passive: He reads the contact like a former colleague: competent, frayed, and hiding nerves. He knows cautious is not the same thing as scared.

discover.text: She half-believes the danger is real and half-suspects she is being used.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: Talking shop as ex-security can earn candor faster than anyone else.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Garrick, your security instincts say the contact is competent and scared, not just cautious.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Protection, reach, weight-sense, terrain scale, and standing between harm and the crew.
perCharacterLayer.passive: She sizes the crate by weight and reach. It is heavier and denser than wood and trade goods, more like stone or metal.
perCharacterLayer.contribute: She can volunteer to carry or guard the crate and claim the protector role before trouble starts.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Khari, by the way the crate sits and the way people handle it, you can tell it is heavier and denser than ordinary cargo.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Heightened smell and hearing, tracking, pathfinding, and home-terrain instinct.
perCharacterLayer.passive: Katari nose: under the leather and road dust, they catch a faint mineral-ozone scent off the crate, like stone that has been somewhere it should not.

discover.text: Varian only: they place the scent as the same wrong-mineral smell tied to deep-preserve sites.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: They know enough about forest routes to advise the road ahead and reduce travel danger.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Varian, your nose catches something nobody else does: a faint mineral-ozone scent from the sealed crate, like stone from somewhere it should not be.

player.title: The briefing is playable
player.statement: Players can question the contact, inspect the package, and choose how they leave.
player.body: Keep the scene active. The players should leave knowing they made the job concrete, even if they did not solve the mystery.
player.say: "This is not a cutscene. Ask the contact what you need to know, inspect what you can see, and decide how your character enters the job."
player.ask: If players ask what options matter: "Ask about pay, route, danger, destination, employer, package handling, who drives, where you sit, and whether anyone checks the crate before departure."
player.deeper: Keep the scene active. The players should leave knowing they made the job concrete, even if they did not solve the mystery.

story.title: The job becomes physical
story.statement: Contact, carriage, package, destination, pay, and unease all become visible.
story.body: A direct roleplay read can give the emotional clue. For sharper detail, use Instinct or Presence 13, or Knowledge 14 for the route story.
story.say: "Now the contract has a person, a carriage, a sealed crate, a route, and a deadline."
story.ask: If players ask what feels off: "The contact is too competent to be casual and too nervous to be merely bored. The route story sounds rehearsed."
story.deeper: A direct roleplay read can give the emotional clue. For sharper detail, use Instinct or Presence 13, or Knowledge 14 for the route story.

mechanic.title: Ask, inspect, read, decide
mechanic.statement: The scene teaches the core loop before danger starts.
mechanic.body: This is the first working demonstration of Daggerheart's fiction-first procedure: player intent creates the roll, not a menu of checks.
mechanic.say: "Ask what you ask, inspect what you inspect, and tell me what your character is watching for. I will answer, call for a roll, or hand the spotlight to the next player."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for the likely rolls: "Instinct or Presence 13 reads the contact. Knowledge 14 reads the route story. Marlowe gets a Knowledge 13 wardcraft read on the crate. Varian can use Instinct 13 for scent."
mechanic.deeper: This is the first working demonstration of Daggerheart's fiction-first procedure: player intent creates the roll, not a menu of checks.

gmBeats.label: Meet the contact
gmBeats.title: Your Contact
gmBeats.gmScript: Use this beat for Sabine only if you want the optional backup NPC job-giver. If Sabine is in play, do not say her name until the players ask or she introduces herself. Push her image to the player display here. Marlowe remains a PC custodian in the crew and receives the job with everyone else.
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: The contact is a real, frayed person, not just a corporate mouthpiece.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: Model the core loop: ask a question, get an answer.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: The woman has a name once I engage with her.

player.title: Engagement reveals the contact
player.statement: The contact has a name when players ask or she introduces herself.
player.body: If Marlowe is a PC, do not make Marlowe the briefer. Marlowe receives the job with everyone else and can still carry custodian pressure.
player.say: "A tired, well-dressed field agent watches the crew from beside the carriage. She looks ready to talk, but she has not volunteered much yet."
player.ask: If players ask her name: "Sabine. Sabine Quillon. You are the crew Emeris sent? Good. We are losing daylight."
player.deeper: If Marlowe is a PC, do not make Marlowe the briefer. Marlowe receives the job with everyone else and can still carry custodian pressure.

story.title: The contact is nervous but capable
story.statement: The contact's tension gives the company story a human crack.
story.body: Do not reveal manufactured danger here. The useful clue is emotional: competence plus nerves.
story.say: "She is not falling apart. She is competent, tired, and watching the road like it has disappointed her before."
story.ask: If players ask whether she is lying: "On Instinct or Presence 13, she is not simply lying; she is repeating a company-safe version of danger while worrying about the parts she cannot control."
story.deeper: Do not reveal manufactured danger here. The useful clue is emotional: competence plus nerves.

mechanic.title: Social reads follow player approach
mechanic.statement: Reading the contact uses Instinct; pressing or reassuring her uses Presence.
mechanic.body: On Fear, give the truth with pressure: she notices the read, gets guarded, or hurries the handoff.
mechanic.say: "If you watch her tells, roll Instinct. If you press, charm, or reassure her, roll Presence. Difficulty 13 either way."
mechanic.ask: If players ask what success gives: "You learn she is scared of the run, not of you, and that the official danger line sounds practiced."
mechanic.deeper: On Fear, give the truth with pressure: she notices the read, gets guarded, or hurries the handoff.

gmBeats.label: Briefing
gmBeats.title: The Sealed Package
gmBeats.gmScript: The briefing lays out the job in plain terms. If Sabine is in play, she gives this information; otherwise keep the same facts without making Marlowe the hirer. The crate is the package, never the Keystone Asset. If asked, the briefer can name Hush and the Sablewood preserve.
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: The contract terms are now explicit and table-facing.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: Foreshadow that the journey will ask for rolls once risk appears.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: I know the objective, the pay condition, and the don't-open-it rule.

player.title: The package is inspectable but sealed
player.statement: Players can examine the outside without opening it.
player.body: This cue should produce action: who checks the seal, who watches the contact, who positions near the cargo.
player.say: "The crate is visible in the carriage: banded shut, cold at the hinges, and not marked for public handling."
player.ask: If players ask whether they can inspect it: "Yes, the outside. You can look, touch, weigh, smell, or check the seal without opening it."
player.deeper: This cue should produce action: who checks the seal, who watches the contact, who positions near the cargo.

story.title: The crate feels more important than cargo
story.statement: The package hints at wardcraft, mineral wrongness, and official handling.
story.body: Even a success should preserve the reveal. Say wardcraft, stone-like weight, wrong mineral, protective seal; do not say Keystone Asset.
story.say: "It looks like cargo until you pay attention; then it looks like cargo someone paid magic and paperwork to keep quiet."
story.ask: If players ask what an inspection reveals: "Knowledge 14: the seal is contractual and protective. Marlowe Knowledge 13: old, high-tier wardcraft. Varian Instinct 13: wrong-mineral scent under the wax. Khari Strength or Instinct 13: the weight sits low and dense, like stone hidden in freight."
story.deeper: Even a success should preserve the reveal. Say wardcraft, stone-like weight, wrong mineral, protective seal; do not say Keystone Asset.

mechanic.title: Inspection uses approach-based traits
mechanic.statement: The trait depends on how the PC investigates.
mechanic.body: This is a strong teaching moment for Daggerheart traits: the same object can invite different traits based on method.
mechanic.say: "Tell me how you inspect it. Reading the magic is Knowledge. Noticing scent or pressure is Instinct. Testing weight is Strength or Instinct."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for Difficulty: "Use 14 for a general inspection, 13 for a character-specific lane: Marlowe wardcraft, Varian scent, Khari weight-sense."
mechanic.deeper: This is a strong teaching moment for Daggerheart traits: the same object can invite different traits based on method.

gmBeats.label: Questions
gmBeats.title: What Do You Ask?
gmBeats.gmScript: Let players interrogate the job. If Sabine is present, use her answers: name if asked; Emeris as employer; Hush as the destination; the forest danger as the company line; sealed means sealed. Marlowe's player also gets bonus insight and an extra Arcana check here.
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: Players convert unknowns into knowns by asking.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: Optional Instinct or Presence 13 can read her nerves; optional Knowledge 14 can sense the official route story is too smooth.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: Curiosity pays, and some answers may feel interestingly incomplete.

player.title: Questions move the scene
player.statement: Players can ask direct practical questions before accepting the road.
player.body: Give the table permission to be concrete. This beat is where players learn that curiosity pays.
player.say: "She is willing to talk while the crew loads up. Ask the practical question your character would not leave without asking."
player.ask: If players ask what to ask: "Who are you? Who hired us? Where are we going? What is the route? What happens if the package is damaged? What danger are you not saying plainly?"
player.deeper: Give the table permission to be concrete. This beat is where players learn that curiosity pays.

story.title: The company line has weak spots
story.statement: Answers provide names and practical facts, plus one useful doubt.
story.body: Names are safe here because the players earned them through the briefing. After naming, immediately translate back into plain meaning: company, village, old forest.
story.say: "Her answers are practical: destination, route, pay, and handoff. The uncomfortable part is how rehearsed the safety language sounds."
story.ask: If players ask for names: "Employer: Emeris Crown Holdings. Destination: Hush, a forest village. Route: the old forest road; company maps call it Sablewood."
story.deeper: Names are safe here because the players earned them through the briefing. After naming, immediately translate back into plain meaning: company, village, old forest.

mechanic.title: Question answers can trigger focused rolls
mechanic.statement: Direct questions get direct answers; hidden pressure gets a roll.
mechanic.body: This cue teaches that rolls should add leverage or texture, not block basic information.
mechanic.say: "If you ask a practical question, she answers. If you want to know what is underneath the answer, that is where a roll can happen."
mechanic.ask: If players ask what roll fits: "Knowledge 14 spots the route story as too clean. Instinct or Presence 13 reads her nerves. On Hope, she volunteers one extra practical detail. On Fear, she answers but gets guarded or pushes the crew to leave."
mechanic.deeper: This cue teaches that rolls should add leverage or texture, not block basic information.

gmBeats.label: Departure
gmBeats.title: You In?
gmBeats.gmScript: Get a clear yes or boarding moment. If Sabine is in play, this is where her backup job-giver role ends. Either way, the whole crew has received the job together and now owns the route.
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: The job is accepted and the journey begins.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: Commitment and fictional positioning are the mechanic: players choose to board, inspect, ask, or create risk before departure.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: We are committed and on the road now.

player.title: The crew commits
player.statement: Players choose to board, position, or force one last action before departure.
player.body: This should close the briefing without hard-cutting player agency.
player.say: "Before the carriage rolls, tell me your last practical move: board, take reins, sit by the crate, ask one final question, or inspect one thing."
player.ask: If players ask whether they can delay: "Yes, briefly. One last question or action, then the job needs to move before the route window closes."
player.deeper: This should close the briefing without hard-cutting player agency.

story.title: The route now belongs to the crew
story.statement: Once they leave, the contact recedes and the party owns the job.
story.body: This prevents the backup contact from becoming a guide NPC. The Prologue hands control to the PCs.
story.say: "The handoff is signed. The contact steps back. The carriage, the package, and the road are yours now."
story.ask: If players ask whether Sabine comes with them: "No. She handles the handoff. The crew takes the route from here."
story.deeper: This prevents the backup contact from becoming a guide NPC. The Prologue hands control to the PCs.

mechanic.title: Commitment and positioning lock in
mechanic.statement: The departure records who drives, who guards the crate, and who watches the road.
mechanic.body: If a PC creates risk before departure, call the roll that matches the action. Tampering with the seal should create employer pressure rather than reveal the contents.
mechanic.say: "Who has the reins, who sits closest to the package, and who is watching the road as you leave?"
mechanic.ask: If players ask why it matters: "Those answers decide who gets the first sensory clue, who can react first to the road, and which trait fits if trouble appears."
mechanic.deeper: If a PC creates risk before departure, call the roll that matches the action. Tampering with the seal should create employer pressure rather than reveal the contents.

title: Entering Sablewood
alt: Entering Sablewood scene art for Act 0 - The Contract.
caption: Threshold transition into the ancient forest.
gmGoal: The carriage crosses from city-controlled road into a vast ancient forest and hands off to Act One.
publicObjective: Cross from the contract briefing into the forest road. The next thing ahead blocks the path.
readAloud: The last warded marker slips behind you. Ahead, the road narrows and the old forest closes around the carriage.
gmNotes: Ask one player what comforting lie a corporate sign tells travelers. Use their answer later as irony.
Keep player-facing information actionable. Reveal systemic truth through objects, reactions, and consequences before naming it.
Manufactured-threat lens: seed the contradiction, do not explain it. The surface goal stays simple and heroic.
gmScript: The last warded marker slips behind you. The road narrows, the city noise thins, and the forest rises around the carriage like a green wall. Who has the reins, and what is the first strange detail your character notices about these trees?
gmChecklist: Ask who is driving the carriage.
Ask one player what is unique about these trees.
Move to the blocked road before the threshold becomes a full travel scene.
gmPrivate: The signs and warded marker are quiet seeds: safety here is built, branded, and sold.
Act One should begin with the Vendor Cart, not another orientation slide.
playerTakeaway: The setting has changed; the forest is now part of the story.
storyTakeaway: The party leaves managed civilization for a living place the company only claims to control.
mechanicTakeaway: Ask one worldbuilding prompt. The first action roll arrives in the next scene.

Incident Response Placard™: A flat brass disc on a post holds a watchful glyph and a single cheerful bell. When trouble happens nearby, the glyph lights, the bell rings once, brightly, and then nothing else happens at all.

storyScope.antagonist_line: Perceived antagonist: the forest. True antagonist: the corporate lie about the forest. The players never confront it directly. They are meant to feel it by the end.
storyScope.gm_thesis: Every act offers at least one guaranteed and one earned hint that the danger is manufactured and the forest is not the enemy.

act_seeds.text: Grail-branded bounty board: "STRIXWOLF: APEX FOREST HAZARD. Sightings up 300%. Bounty payable in Marks."
Couriers or a clerk trade fearful route gossip: the Preserve "takes one a week now."
A player asking what they know receives the corporate line: strixwolves are vicious pack predators.

roll_menu: Knowledge Easy 10: recall the corporate strixwolf line if asked.

pacing.label: Onboarding + Prologue
pacing.context: pregens, safety, connections, Contract overview, Job briefing, forest threshold
pacing.lever: Keep the Contract to plain setup, let the Job carry questions, then move to the blocked road.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Arcana, ward-sense, and the custodian responsibility around the package.
perCharacterLayer.passive: Her attuned elven senses pick up faint ambient magic from the warded marker as they cross. She feels the boundary click off behind them.
perCharacterLayer.contribute: She can name that the boundary felt built, maintained, and contractual rather than natural.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Marlowe, as the last marker passes behind you, you feel a faint magical boundary click shut like a latch.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Shadows, deals, underworld instinct, and noticing when a job smells wrong.
perCharacterLayer.passive: The treeline has good shadow cover. He is already mapping where he would hide, or where someone else would.

discover.text: He spots that the official road is suspiciously the only cleared path; everything else has grown over.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: He can call out hiding places before the carriage reaches a blind curve.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Barnacle, the treeline is full of hiding places. The official road is almost too clean compared with everything grown over around it.

perCharacterLayer.ancestryClass: Highborne Human Warrior, Call of the Brave
perCharacterLayer.lane: Threat-reading, escort habits, social warmth, and de-escalation.
perCharacterLayer.passive: Sightlines. He clocks the road's blind corners before the party reaches them, an old escort habit.
perCharacterLayer.contribute: He can ask who is watching the curve, the rear, and the carriage before the first blockage.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Garrick, your old escort habits kick in. The road has blind corners before the carriage reaches them.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Protection, reach, weight-sense, terrain scale, and standing between harm and the crew.
perCharacterLayer.passive: The scale of the trees registers differently to a giant. She reads them as climbable, defensible, useful terrain, not just scenery.
perCharacterLayer.contribute: She can point out where a large body can brace, lift, block, or climb if trouble hits.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Khari, these trees are not just scenery to you. At this size, they are climbable, defensible, and useful.

perCharacterLayer.lane: Heightened smell and hearing, tracking, pathfinding, and home-terrain instinct.
perCharacterLayer.passive: This is their world. Varian reads the forest's mood through scent and sound. The hybrid animals are calm now, which means nothing is hunting yet.

discover.text: They pinpoint which direction the lark-moths and fox-bats avoid, foreshadowing the road blockage ahead.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: Wayfinder gives the GM a clean reason to frame the fastest safe line through this stretch.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Varian, the forest is calm for now. You can hear small creatures moving normally, which means nothing is hunting yet.

player.title: The table crosses a threshold
player.statement: Players know the setting has changed and the forest matters.
player.body: This transition should be brief, sensory, and playable. It is not a second lore briefing.
player.say: "The city falls behind. The road narrows. The old forest becomes the room around the carriage."
player.ask: If players ask what to do here: "Tell me who has the reins, where your character is in the carriage, and one thing they notice as the trees close in."
player.deeper: This transition should be brief, sensory, and playable. It is not a second lore briefing.

story.title: The company does not own the old forest
story.statement: The forest feels older and larger than the signs claiming it.
story.body: Use size and sensory language first: trunks wider than a carriage, green filtered light, animal calls dropping quiet, brass signs bolted to older stone.
story.say: "The signs say the route is managed. The trees make that claim feel very small."
story.ask: If players ask what the forest is called: "Locals call it the old forest. The company signs call it Sablewood."
story.deeper: Use size and sensory language first: trunks wider than a carriage, green filtered light, animal calls dropping quiet, brass signs bolted to older stone.

mechanic.title: Threshold framing hands players authorship
mechanic.statement: Ask who drives and let one player add a concrete forest detail.
mechanic.body: This reinforces that players can author sensory details when invited, while Kyle keeps control of hidden causes and the next obstacle.
mechanic.say: "Before the road problem appears, who has the reins, and what is one strange detail your character notices about these trees?"
mechanic.ask: If players ask for a roll: "Most details are free. Use Instinct 10 if someone wants a hint of trouble before the next scene; success points toward where the forest goes quiet."
mechanic.deeper: This reinforces that players can author sensory details when invited, while Kyle keeps control of hidden causes and the next obstacle.

playerBeats.label: Threshold
playerBeats.title: The Old Forest
playerBeats.alt: A carriage enters a colossal green forest road.
playerBeats.caption: The road narrows under trees the size of houses.
playerBeats.publicObjective: The last warded marker slides past: a carved stone pillar with brass company stamps bolted to its face. Open country closes into forest. The trees are wrong in scale, trunks wider than the carriage, rising until the canopy swallows the sky. Behind you, the city. Ahead, green light and a long quiet road.
playerBeats.readAloud: The last warded marker slides past: a carved stone pillar with brass company stamps bolted to its face. Open country closes into forest. The trees are wrong in scale, trunks wider than the carriage, rising until the canopy swallows the sky. Behind you, the city. Ahead, green light and a long quiet road.

playerBeats.label: First impressions
playerBeats.title: Green Light
playerBeats.alt: Entering Sablewood scene art for Act 0 - The Contract.
playerBeats.publicObjective: From inside the carriage you can hear the forest living around you: low calls in the canopy, croaks in the wet dark, small bodies scattering through underbrush. The light comes down green and filtered. Whatever this place agreed to, it did not agree to be owned.
playerBeats.readAloud: From inside the carriage you can hear the forest living around you: low calls in the canopy, croaks in the wet dark, small bodies scattering through underbrush. The light comes down green and filtered. Whatever this place agreed to, it did not agree to be owned.

playerBeats.title: Something Blocks The Path
playerBeats.alt: Entering Sablewood scene art for Act 0 - The Contract.

playerBeats.readAloud: The road bends ahead, tight around a stand of trees. Your driver eases the carriage into the curve, and something is blocking the path.

gmBeats.label: Threshold
gmBeats.title: The Old Forest
gmBeats.gmScript: The trees are bigger than the road was built for. If someone asks what this place is called, say, 'Locals call it the old forest. The company signs call it Sablewood.'
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: They cross from the safe, branded world into the old forest.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: Threshold framing is the mechanic: mark the boundary, ask who has the reins, and let one player author a concrete forest detail.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: We have crossed a threshold.

player.title: The old forest arrives visually
player.statement: Players see scale, green light, and the last managed marker behind them.
player.body: This cue is a sensory handoff from civilization to wild scale.
player.say: "The last warded marker slips behind you. Ahead, trunks wider than the carriage rise until the canopy swallows the sky."
player.ask: If players ask what the marker says: "It is a company road marker bolted over older stone. The new brass wants you to trust the route; the old stone looks like it was here first."
player.deeper: This cue is a sensory handoff from civilization to wild scale.

story.title: Managed safety starts to feel thin
story.statement: The route's official safety markers are newer than the place they mark.
story.body: This plants the corporate-overwrite theme without explaining it.
story.say: "The road is maintained, but the maintenance feels recent. The forest does not."
story.ask: If players inspect the road or signs: "Give the clue plainly: the road is older than the signage nailed beside it."
story.deeper: This plants the corporate-overwrite theme without explaining it.

mechanic.title: Boundary, driver, first-noticer
mechanic.statement: The threshold decides who is physically positioned for the next scene.
mechanic.body: A roll here should foreshadow, not solve. The next slide still carries the first concrete obstacle.
mechanic.say: "Who has the reins as the marker passes behind you, and who is looking out from the carriage?"
mechanic.ask: If players ask what a roll could do: "Instinct 10 can catch that the forest sounds pull away from one direction, foreshadowing the blockage ahead."
mechanic.deeper: A roll here should foreshadow, not solve. The next slide still carries the first concrete obstacle.

gmBeats.label: First impressions
gmBeats.title: Green Light
gmBeats.gmScript: You've noticed something unique about the trees here. What is it? And who is driving when the road begins to feel too narrow for the carriage?
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: The forest is alive and strange, not just a travel lane.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: This reinforces player-authored world detail. Optional Instinct 10 can foreshadow trouble.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: I can help build the place with one concrete detail.

player.title: Players can add one forest detail
player.statement: The table helps make the forest vivid with one concrete observation.
player.body: This is a safe creativity prompt: small, sensory, optional, and bounded.
player.say: "Give me one concrete detail your character notices: sound, smell, light, motion, temperature, or something about the trees."
player.ask: If a player freezes: "You can take one of mine: green light, wet bark smell, animal calls above you, roots like old hands, or a road too narrow for comfort."
player.deeper: This is a safe creativity prompt: small, sensory, optional, and bounded.

story.title: The forest is alive, not scenery
story.statement: The place reacts through sound, scale, and quiet.
story.body: Use per-character hooks to distribute attention without making every moment a roll.
story.say: "The forest is not a backdrop. It has weather, breath, animals, and old paths under the company road."
story.ask: If players ask what their PC senses: "Varian catches layered smells first; Barnacle notices what would make a good hiding place; Garrick reads the road like security exposure; Khari feels how small the carriage is under the trees; Marlowe notices wardcraft fading behind them."
story.deeper: Use per-character hooks to distribute attention without making every moment a roll.

mechanic.title: Sensory spotlight can become Instinct
mechanic.statement: Free description becomes an Instinct roll only when the player pushes for warning.
mechanic.body: On Fear, still give the warning but make it late, partial, or unnerving.
mechanic.say: "A sensory detail is free. If you are trying to read danger from it, roll Instinct."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for Difficulty: "Instinct 10 gives a broad warning that sound thins near the bend. Varian gets the clearest direction on success because scent and hearing are their lane."
mechanic.deeper: On Fear, still give the warning but make it late, partial, or unnerving.

gmBeats.label: Hand-off
gmBeats.title: Something Blocks The Path
gmBeats.gmScript: The road bends tight around a stand of ancient trunks. As the carriage comes through the curve, something is blocking the path.
gmBeats.storyTakeaway: The quiet road delivers its first complication.
gmBeats.mechanicTakeaway: Next scene brings the first action pressure.
gmBeats.playerTakeaway: The adventure proper has started.

player.title: The first obstacle is about to enter
player.statement: Players understand the quiet road is becoming active play.
player.body: This cue is the handoff, not the whole encounter. It should create forward pull.
player.say: "The carriage eases around the bend, and something is blocking the path."
player.ask: If players ask what they see: "Hold that for the next scene: shapes on the road, the carriage slowing, and enough time for one immediate reaction."
player.deeper: This cue is the handoff, not the whole encounter. It should create forward pull.

story.title: The route complication arrives
story.statement: The delivery is no longer only a contract; the road now pushes back.
story.body: Keep identity withheld until the Act One scene starts. Description first, proper nouns later.
story.say: "Whatever the company promised, the road has its own first answer."
story.ask: If players ask whether this is an ambush: "Your characters do not know yet. You know the path is blocked and the carriage is losing easy forward motion."
story.deeper: Keep identity withheld until the Act One scene starts. Description first, proper nouns later.

mechanic.title: Cut on pressure
mechanic.statement: The mechanic is pacing: end the Prologue on the first actionable pressure.
mechanic.body: This protects pacing and prevents the threshold from absorbing the Act One encounter.
mechanic.say: "Pause there. That is our handoff into the first road problem."
mechanic.ask: If players ask for an immediate reaction: "You can call out, grab the reins, move toward the package, or look ahead. The next scene will resolve what that means."
mechanic.deeper: This protects pacing and prevents the threshold from absorbing the Act One encounter.

sensorySummary: Corporate route signs, liability placards, and numbered posts sit against trunks wide enough to make the signage look temporary.

locationSlideModel.gmOrientation: The frame the entire adventure rides through: a colossal old-growth forest that Kazrak Industries claims to steward but never truly owned. It is the connective tissue between every other location — the carriage is always in the Preserve. Use it to set tone, plant unease, and answer "what's around us?" between scenes.
locationSlideModel.readAloud: This evening your party finally reaches the Sablewood Logistics Preserve — a sprawl of trees older than any signed deed, their trunks rising hundreds of feet until the canopy swallows the sky. The road beneath your carriage was a trade path long before Kazrak Industries stamped its name on it. From inside, you hear the forest breathing around you: the low call of lark-moths, the croak of a lemur-toad, the scatter of a fox-bat family through the underbrush. The light comes down green and filtered. Whatever this place agreed to, it did not agree to be owned.

sensoryStack.detail: Trees too large to be plausible; brass Kazrak compliance stamps nailed into bark and already being grown over; sunken trade paths worn into the roots; faint courier-route markers.
Lark-moth calls, lemur-toad croaks, fox-bat scittering, the creak of the carriage, wind moving through a canopy so high you never see it move.
Wet bark, crushed greenery, a sweetness like overripe fruit underneath. a faint resin tang near the compliance stamps.
Cool, damp, heavier than open road. Light arrives green.
Hybrid animals are the Preserve's signature — lark-moths, lemur-toads, fox-bats, and (later) strixwolves. NPCs are rare on the road itself; this is between-towns wilderness.

sensorySummary: Ancient trunks lean over the road until the sky becomes a thin green seam; old stones and moss shelves guide travel better than signs.
Leaf-drip, distant wingbeats, branches rubbing like low speech, and bird calls that restart behind the party but not ahead.
Cold rain on leaves, fungal sweetness, sap, wet bark, and the musk of unseen animals moving through root-shadow.
Bark leaves dark moisture and gold-brown pollen on fingers; the road shifts from springy moss to slick clay underfoot.
Owls, insects, and small ground creatures are around, but their silence moves like a ripple when danger or corporate residue passes.
visibleDetails: Great trunks lean over the road until the sky feels rationed.
Old stones, root shelves, and moss-dark bends shape travel more than signs do.
subtleDetails: Animals are present, but not where the signs say they should be.
Some roots curl around waymarker nails as if rejecting them slowly.
hazards: Lore sprawl. Keep as texture and move on.

title: Act One: The Logistics Incident
caption: The branded route stops feeling managed when the Old Sable answers back.
gmGoal: Open Act 1 as the first road complication: the routine courier job stops, the forest feels dangerous, and the first real rolls become possible.
publicObjective: Get the carriage and the sealed package moving again, then continue through the preserve toward the village.
readAloud: The warded city is behind you now. The road runs on under a canopy so high you never see it move, and the carriage rocks along ruts older than any company that claims this forest. The job is simple: deliver the package, get paid. The forest, so far, has other ideas.
playerTakeaway: You are past the point of no return; the only paid direction is forward through the preserve.

title: The Overturned Vendor Cart
alt: The Overturned Vendor Cart scene art for The Logistics Incident.
caption: The overturned cart gives the party a mystery before it gives them a fight.
gmGoal: Block the road with a wrecked vendor cart, let the table read the scene, and plant that the obvious animal story does not add up.
publicObjective: Figure out what happened here and clear the road.
readAloud: Your steeds haul the carriage around a tight bend and stop hard. The path ahead is blocked: a vendor cart lies overturned, its fruit, vegetables, and spilled preserves scattered across the trail. Something has been feeding here. The air is wrong: sweet rot and something underneath it, coppery. From the far side of the cart, you hear wet, unhurried movement.
gmNotes: Use the wreck as an investigation scene first and a creature reveal second.
Player-safe language: body, feeding, blade wound. GM-only truth: staged murder and later Bramble connection.
gmScript: Say: "The carriage stops hard. Ahead of you is a wreck, a body, and something feeding just out of sight. You can rush toward the sound, but you have time to look first. What do you check?" If someone checks the body, say: "The feeding is messy, but the killing wound is clean. This was not done by claws." If they need the roll, call Knowledge or Instinct, Difficulty 12.
gmReadAloud: The path ahead is blocked: a vendor cart lies overturned, its fruit, vegetables, and spilled preserves scattered across the trail.
Something has been feeding here. Sweet rot hangs over the copper smell of blood.
From the far side of the cart, you hear wet, unhurried movement.
gmChecklist: Offer investigation before the creature fully reveals.
Gate the slit-throat truth behind Garrick's passive read or a Knowledge/Instinct 12 check.
Seed the deliberate bramble in the wheel if Barnacle searches the cart.
Move to S01-03 when they approach the far side, try to clear the cart, or make enough noise to draw the creature out.
gmPrivate: The driver was murdered with a blade, then the scene was staged to read as a forest attack.
The creature is scavenging. It did not make the killing wound.
The bramble in the wheel foreshadows the later ambush. Seed it; do not explain it.
playerTakeaway: Someone is dead, the road is blocked, and something alive is feeding on the other side of the cart.
storyTakeaway: The wreck looks like a wild-animal attack, but the clean wound and staged cart point to a person behind the violence.
mechanicTakeaway: Investigation begins with what a PC examines; roll Knowledge or Instinct only when the answer is uncertain or gated.

Keystone Asset™: Inside the sealed crate, packed in wax-paper and reassurance, sits a heavy grey stone the size of a loaf, warm to the touch, faintly humming, with a light deep inside it that is slowly going out.

Incident Response Placard™: A flat brass disc on a post holds a watchful glyph and a single cheerful bell. When trouble happens nearby, the glyph lights, the bell rings once, brightly, and then nothing else happens at all.

Sableblade: Growing straight up out of dark forest soil, like a sapling that decided to be a sword, is a blade of living dark wood and pale metal. It has no maker's mark and hums when your hand nears the hilt.
Recall Stone: A smooth grey pebble feels warm and ordinary until it refuses to stay where you put it. Set it down, look away, and it waits back in your palm.
Goldwater Liability Token™: A heavy brass chit with a smiling coin-face drops into your palm like a tiny verdict. The fine print is too small to read without feeling blamed.

perCharacterLayer.passive: The blood under the sweet-rot smell is older than the creature's feeding. Other PCs just smell that something is wrong.

discover.text: Places animal musk as recent, human blood as older, and a faint chemical-leather tang that belongs to neither.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: Can track which direction the creature came from versus which direction the killer left.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Varian, your nose sorts this out faster than the others. The blood here is older than the animal. Want to follow what that tells you?

perCharacterLayer.passive: The throat wound is a clean blade cut, not claws or teeth. Someone killed this man.

discover.text: Confirms a deliberate, practiced cut: an execution staged as an animal attack.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: Can secure the scene and keep the party calm and methodical.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Garrick, you have stood over bodies before. This one's wrong. Want to say how?

perCharacterLayer.passive: The cart was tipped from the wrong side to be a simple accident.

discover.text: Finds thorny bramble wedged in the carriage wheel and valuables stripped before the creature arrived.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: Can rig the cart to clear the road quickly or quietly pocket something useful from the wreck.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Barnacle, this does not read like an accident to you. What do you notice?

perCharacterLayer.passive: From her height she sees the drag marks, the feeding place, and the death place are not the same spot.
perCharacterLayer.contribute: Can clear the overturned cart single-handed when the party is ready to move.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Khari, you can see the whole picture from up there. The man did not die where he is being eaten. Want to point that out?

perCharacterLayer.passive: Her attuned senses register no magic on the scene. Whatever happened here was mundane and deliberate.

discover.text: Confirms the absence of magic is notable; this killing was done the old-fashioned way by someone using the wild as cover.

perCharacterLayer.contribute: Can tell the party that the important package is not what caused this wreck to pulse with magic; there is no pulse here.
perCharacterLayer.playerCue: Marlowe, you would feel it if magic did this. You do not. That is worth sitting with.

player.title: Player takeaway
player.statement: Someone is dead, the road is blocked, and something alive is feeding on the other side of the cart.
player.say: "Three facts: someone is dead, the road is blocked, and something is eating on the other side of that cart. What do you do?"
player.ask: "You can search the cart, approach the body, listen to the thing feeding, hang back and watch, or ask another PC what they notice."
player.deeper: Give the table four concrete entry points: cart, body, sound, or position. This prevents the scene from becoming a single forced monster reveal.

story.title: Story takeaway
story.statement: The wreck looks like a wild-animal attack, but the clean wound and staged cart point to a person behind the violence.
story.say: "At first glance, this reads like the kind of forest attack the company warns about. The closer you look, the less clean that story gets."
story.ask: "The obvious answer is a creature attack. The discoverable answer is that the driver was killed with a blade first. Knowledge or Instinct 12 confirms it."
story.deeper: Do not name the later faction connection to players. Let the first fact stand: animal scavenging is true, but animal murder is false.

mechanic.title: Mechanic takeaway
mechanic.statement: Investigation begins with what a PC examines; roll Knowledge or Instinct only when the answer is uncertain or gated.
mechanic.say: "Tell me what you examine. If the answer is obvious, I will give it to you. If the answer is uncertain or needs expertise, I will name the trait and the difficulty."
mechanic.ask: "Searching the cart gives basic facts automatically. Reading the cause of death is Knowledge or Instinct, Difficulty 12. Spotting deliberate staging in the wheel is Instinct, Difficulty 13."
mechanic.deeper: This is the first investigation procedure: question, object, answer. Dice appear only when the table needs uncertainty, expertise, or consequence.

sensorySummary: A torn canvas cart, scattered cargo, wheel ruts, a body placed too neatly, and feathered movement low under the wreck.
A low wing-rustle under the cart, spooked horses breathing hard, small pups shifting in cover, and the forest holding back its usual calls.
Coppery blood, wet road grit, torn grain sacks, animal musk, and rain soaking into canvas.
Mud is churned and slick near the wheels; the cart boards are splintered; loose feathers cling to wet hands.
The strixwolf family is alive, frightened, and watching. The corpse and staging are evidence; the animal pressure is a mercy test.

The dead driver: throat slit by a blade, then partially fed on.
The carriage wheel: thorny bramble deliberately wedged in it.
The spilled produce and preserves: harmless, but the sweet rot masks the blood smell.
The underbrush: movement, pups, and the creature's protected space.
hazards: Strixwolf protective pressure
spooked horses
hidden Bramble evidence

locationSlideModel.gmOrientation: The inciting scene and the table's first action roll (a Presence check to read the strixwolf). An overturned vendor cart blocks the road; a strixwolf and her pups are feeding on the dead driver. It teaches the Duality Dice through a tense-but-survivable animal encounter, and quietly plants the murder mystery (the driver's neck was slit — this was no accident).
locationSlideModel.readAloud: As your steeds haul the carriage around a tight corner, the path ahead is blocked. A vendor cart lies overturned, fruits and vegetables scattered across the trail. From behind it steps a strixwolf — a large creature with the body of a wolf, the face of an owl, broad wings folded along its back. It is finishing a meal: the hand of the dead driver. It stares at you, unhurried, deciding whether you are friend or food. Behind it, two pups stumble clumsily into view. Inside, you feel the carriage lurch to a halt. What do you do?

sensoryStack.detail: Overturned cart, scattered produce, the dead driver, the owl-faced wolf, two pups, broad feathered wings.
The strixwolf's wet chewing, a low warning hoot-howl, pups mewling, produce squelching underfoot.
blood and crushed fruit together — sweet and iron, deeply wrong.
Sudden stillness; the carriage stopped; everyone's breath held.
The strixwolf family is the focus. fox-bats watch from branches, drawn by the spilled food.

Canon scenario (p.30): stripped of valuables; driver's arm mangled by the family.
Canon (p.30): the driver's neck was slit. This is the murder seed — Bramble Union foreshadow.
Canon (p.30): on success, deal weapon damage; pups flee; mother flies to a branch and watches.
